items.title: Tighter chip controls from the target's side
items.scene: Restrictions tighten again on advanced chips and tooling. In Beijing, officials are deciding what deserves priority next: domestic substitution, selective outside access, broader ecosystem investment, or restraint against panic.
items.whyHard: Trying to duplicate every bottleneck is costly. Leaving key layers exposed lets foreign governments set the ceiling on future capacity.

contextBullets.label: Actor role
contextBullets.text: Answer from the target state's industrial-policy position, not from Washington's preferred line.

contextBullets.label: Crisis stage
contextBullets.text: Restrictions are tightening, but Chinese firms still retain some access, workarounds, and investment room.

contextBullets.label: Immediate constraint
contextBullets.text: China wants to reduce exposure without wasting capital on every symbolic bottleneck at once.

contextBullets.label: Uncertainty
contextBullets.text: It is unclear whether the main danger is short-run capability loss, long-run dependency, or overreaction.

options.title: Accelerate domestic substitution
options.label: The first job is to replace foreign choke points even if the near-term cost is high.

options.title: Protect access where you still can
options.label: Selective cooperation, narrower retaliation, and targeted diplomacy may preserve room that a full break would destroy.

options.title: Build the wider ecosystem
options.label: The real priority is talent, tools, power, finance, and manufacturing depth, not chasing every frontier bottleneck at once.

options.title: Do not turn every gap into an emergency
options.label: Panic can waste resources and harden blocs faster than the restrictions themselves.

items.title: Releasing a powerful open-weight model
items.prompt: What should govern the release decision?
items.scene: A frontier lab is considering releasing a powerful model with weights that others could freely download and modify. Advocates point to research diffusion and broader access; critics warn about misuse, proliferation, and the difficulty of containing highly capable systems once the weights are public.
items.whyHard: The same release can widen innovation and widen misuse at the same time, so the question is which risk should anchor the policy line.

contextBullets.label: Actor / stake
contextBullets.text: Labs, governments, researchers, and smaller developers do not bear the gains and risks of release equally.

contextBullets.label: Uncertainty
contextBullets.text: It is unclear where targeted openness ends and uncontrolled proliferation begins.

options.title: Restrict above threshold
options.label: Once capability crosses a line, broad release stops being a normal research choice and becomes a misuse and security problem.

options.title: Use staged release
options.label: Access can stay broad, but only through common testing, security baselines, and release protocols that others can also adopt.

options.title: Keep access broad
options.label: Locking powerful models behind a few firms or governments carries its own political and innovation costs. Openness should remain the default.

options.title: Focus on deployers
options.label: The stronger line is to regulate who deploys high-risk systems and how, rather than treating the weights themselves as the whole problem.

items.title: Foreign clouds and sovereign stacks
items.prompt: What is the strongest reading of why some states want a sovereign AI stack?
items.scene: A lower-income state relies on foreign cloud providers, imported data-center hardware, and outside software for most of its digital government functions. Officials are debating local storage rules and a modest sovereign AI stack. Critics call it expensive symbolism. Supporters call it the price of not living inside someone else's infrastructure.
items.whyHard: The same move can be about control, bargaining power, development, or politics. The reason you think is primary changes what policy follows.

contextBullets.label: Actor / stake
contextBullets.text: The state wants digital growth, but it cannot cheaply build every layer itself.

contextBullets.label: Uncertainty
contextBullets.text: Local rules may reduce exposure, or they may just move dependence into a more expensive form.

options.title: It is about control
options.label: The main driver is strategic control over sensitive data, compute, and deployment pathways that states no longer trust outsiders to hold.

options.title: It is about dependence
options.label: The stronger explanation is that states fear being locked into infrastructures they cannot shape when pressure sharpens.

options.title: It is about development room
options.label: For many states the issue is building enough local capacity to avoid permanent digital dependence.

options.title: It is about fragmentation
options.label: The more persuasive reading is that governments are overlearning security language and underestimating the cost of splintering interoperable systems.

items.title: Fab resilience without closing trade
items.prompt: What should carry the most weight in the resilience strategy?
items.scene: A government deeply dependent on Taiwanese and Korean fabs wants more resilience without collapsing open trade. Officials disagree on whether the answer is duplication at home, allied production networks, portfolio redundancy, or simple restraint against overcorrection.
items.whyHard: Concentration at the frontier is risky, but trying to duplicate everything can be wasteful enough to weaken the capacity you are trying to build.

contextBullets.label: Actor / stake
contextBullets.text: The state needs more resilience but cannot cheaply recreate the whole semiconductor stack on its own.

contextBullets.label: Uncertainty
contextBullets.text: There is no clean line between prudent redundancy and politically expensive overbuilding.

options.title: Duplicate more at home
options.label: Frontier concentration is itself the vulnerability. Strategic sectors need more domestic slack even when it is expensive.

options.title: Build trusted networks
options.label: Resilience comes from a broader allied manufacturing map, not every state trying to rebuild the full stack alone.

options.title: Build portfolio depth
options.label: The practical answer is redundancy across design tools, packaging, inventories, and inputs rather than one giant reshoring gesture.

options.title: Avoid overcorrection
options.label: Concentration is risky, but duplicating everything can freeze resources and lock in the wrong industrial bets.

items.title: Compute, cloud, and industrial catch-up
items.prompt: What is the strongest reading of how a middle power should build durable AI capacity?
items.scene: A large middle power is deciding whether compute, cloud, and data centers should be treated as strategic public infrastructure or left mainly to the market. Officials agree the country cannot build every layer of the stack. They disagree on what kind of system actually creates durable advantage.
items.whyHard: If you misread where advantage comes from, you can spend heavily and still stay dependent.

contextBullets.label: Actor / stake
contextBullets.text: The state wants more capacity, but its fiscal room and technical base are limited.

contextBullets.label: Uncertainty
contextBullets.text: It is unclear whether catch-up comes mainly from public buildout, market adaptation, coalition specialization, or protected autonomy.

options.title: Public buildout matters most
options.label: Strategic sectors usually do not appear at the needed scale or speed without public finance and infrastructure.

options.title: Specialization matters most
options.label: The stronger model is to pool scale across partners instead of trying to rebuild the whole stack alone.

options.title: Market adaptation matters most
options.label: Government should set guardrails and basic infrastructure, but heavy planning can lock in the wrong bets.

options.title: Protected depth matters most
options.label: Dependence on foreign capital, cloud, or tools creates future vulnerability. Some domestic depth has to be built and sheltered.

items.title: Public compute and access gaps
items.prompt: What should carry the most weight in the response to access concentration?
items.scene: Universities, startups, and smaller states argue that frontier AI is increasingly shaped by whoever controls the largest compute budgets. Policymakers debate public compute, shared research infrastructure, private scaling, and more development-focused access strategies.
items.whyHard: The frontier is expensive because it is hard, but that does not answer whether concentrated access is merely efficient or politically distorting.

contextBullets.label: Actor / stake
contextBullets.text: Access affects who can do research, train talent, and build downstream capability.

contextBullets.label: Uncertainty
contextBullets.text: A public-access fix can widen participation, but it may still fall short of what the frontier actually costs.

options.title: Build public compute
options.label: If compute stays concentrated in a few private actors, broad research access and public oversight will keep shrinking.

options.title: Share trusted infrastructure
options.label: A network of trusted research clouds can widen access without requiring every state to finance a frontier stack alone.

options.title: Let private scale lead
options.label: The frontier is expensive because it is genuinely difficult. Heavy public intervention may spread resources thin without matching private speed.

options.title: Treat access as development
options.label: The core issue is not only frontier competition. It is whether poorer states and public institutions are being locked out of the next production stack.

items.title: Frontier AI governance
items.scene: Frontier AI capabilities are accelerating. Policymakers debate licensing, compute thresholds, open models, and national-security risk. The underlying dispute is over what kind of governance is strong enough to matter before the field outruns it.
items.whyHard: Move too slowly and guardrails arrive after the capabilities that need them. Move too heavily and you risk locking in the wrong institutions or actors.

contextBullets.label: Actor / stake
contextBullets.text: States want to manage real risk without handing the field by default to a few governments or firms.

contextBullets.label: Uncertainty
contextBullets.text: No one knows whether capability growth will outpace voluntary norms, hard rules, or both.

options.title: Use hard thresholds
options.label: Licensing and compute thresholds are necessary because some risks arrive before markets or informal norms can catch up.

options.title: Govern with capable partners
options.label: The strongest path is shared standards and coordinated restrictions among states that can actually enforce them.

options.title: Keep innovation open
options.label: Heavy gating will entrench incumbents and slow useful progress. Safeguards should stay targeted rather than general.

options.title: Treat capability as strategic
options.label: The first priority is national capability. Governance should not become a back door to long-run self-limitation.

items.title: Military AI deployment
items.prompt: What should carry the most weight in the deployment choice?
items.scene: After a year of rapid battlefield experimentation abroad, a defense ministry is deciding whether to field AI-enabled targeting and battle-management tools before its testing standards are mature. Commanders warn that waiting could leave the force behind a rival. Lawyers and allies warn that rushed deployment could spread unclear doctrine and weak accountability across the coalition.
items.whyHard: Speed and caution are both strategic arguments here, so the choice is not simply innovation versus ethics. The immediate question is what should set the deployment threshold before rough practice becomes coalition doctrine.

contextBullets.label: Actor role
contextBullets.text: You are judging a defense ministry deciding whether to authorize broader deployment now.

contextBullets.label: Crisis stage
contextBullets.text: The technology is moving from limited experimentation toward operational fielding.

contextBullets.label: Immediate constraint
contextBullets.text: Allies may inherit the doctrine and risk before common safeguards are in place.

contextBullets.label: Uncertainty
contextBullets.text: A slower rollout may preserve control, but it may also hand real operational learning to a rival.

options.title: Field before the rival sets the baseline
options.label: A military that waits for high confidence may discover that its rival set the operational baseline first.

options.title: Gate deployment through thresholds
options.label: Deployment can continue, but only through staged testing, auditable logs, and hard limits on autonomous action.

options.title: Set coalition baselines first
options.label: The bigger danger is close partners racing ahead with different thresholds and incompatible doctrine.

options.title: Keep responsibility legible
options.label: The deepest risk combines technical error with the erosion of responsibility once command decisions become opaque.

items.title: AI access from a sanctioned state's side
items.prompt: From this government's side, which logic looks strongest?
items.scene: The usual debate in Washington and major firms is about trusted suppliers, safeguards, and secure access. A sanctions-constrained middle-income state is looking at the same landscape from a different angle: it wants AI compute and cloud access for education, logistics, and public services, but the fastest outside options could also deepen surveillance exposure and political dependence. Its cabinet is deciding which logic best captures its own position before it commits scarce public money.
items.whyHard: What looks like manageable dependence from the outside can look like future coercive vulnerability from the state's side.

contextBullets.label: Actor role
contextBullets.text: This is a pressure test. Answer from the government's own strategic position, not from what Washington, Beijing, or a donor would prefer.

contextBullets.label: Crisis stage
contextBullets.text: This is an early buildout decision, before the state's technical dependence is locked in.

contextBullets.label: Immediate constraint
contextBullets.text: The state cannot finance every layer of the stack, but it still wants room to bargain and protect sensitive systems.

contextBullets.label: Uncertainty
contextBullets.text: It is unclear whether sovereignty, diversification, shared capacity, or simple access is the decisive constraint.

options.title: Treat it as a sovereignty problem
options.label: The main issue is how to build enough domestic depth in data, talent, and cloud access to reduce future coercive vulnerability.

options.title: Treat it as a lock-in problem
options.label: The stronger answer is diversified suppliers and portable standards that keep dependence from hardening into captivity.

options.title: Treat it as a scale problem
options.label: Shared compute, training, and procurement may be the only realistic way to widen room to maneuver.

options.title: Treat it as an access problem
options.label: For many states the bigger danger is being left out of the technology shift altogether, not becoming too dependent within it.

items.title: Nonaligned state under U.S.-China tech pressure
items.prompt: From this government's side, which logic looks strongest?
items.scene: A large nonaligned state is deciding whether to join a new technology-security arrangement after fresh U.S. controls and Chinese retaliation threats. In Washington the case is framed as security. In Beijing it is framed as an attempt to freeze hierarchy. This government has to decide which logic best captures its own strategic read before trade and technology talks begin.
items.whyHard: From the outside, both major powers offer ready-made stories. The government still has to decide which diagnosis matters most for its own room to maneuver.

contextBullets.label: Actor role
contextBullets.text: This is a pressure test. Answer from the government's own strategic position, not from Washington's or Beijing's preferred framing.

contextBullets.label: Crisis stage
contextBullets.text: The controls fight is active, but the government still has room to decide how closely it will align.

contextBullets.label: Immediate constraint
contextBullets.text: The state wants advanced technology access without becoming permanently subordinate to either camp.

contextBullets.label: Uncertainty
contextBullets.text: It is unclear whether the controls are a narrow security measure or part of a longer strategy to preserve hierarchy.

options.title: Strategic denial is real
options.label: Some technologies really do alter the balance of power. Governments will act on that whether rivals call it containment or not.

options.title: Rule design is the issue
options.label: Controls become easier to defend when they are narrow, public, and coordinated rather than sprawling and improvised.

options.title: Hierarchy management is real
options.label: The hierarchy critique is partly right: security concerns can be real and still preserve unequal control over technological advancement.

options.title: Hedging will persist
options.label: Many states will protect room to maneuver because both camps offer leverage and dependency in different forms.

items.title: A fast infrastructure deal that could create lock-in
items.scene: A lower-income state can get fast data-center finance only from one outside provider that would also run cloud security, maintenance, and most public-sector hosting. Ministers must decide what matters most before signing.
items.whyHard: The deal could close a real capacity gap quickly, but it could also lock sensitive systems into one foreign stack.

contextBullets.label: Actor / stake
contextBullets.text: The state wants digital capacity now, but it does not want critical systems to become politically hard to replace later.

contextBullets.label: Uncertainty
contextBullets.text: It is unclear whether the bigger danger is staying underbuilt now or accepting a form of dependence that hardens over time.

options.title: Take the access now
options.label: The immediate capability gap is the first problem. A fast buildout matters more than avoiding every future dependency risk.

options.title: Protect the sensitive layers
options.label: The state should move only if it keeps firmer control over security, data, and the parts of the stack that would be hardest to unwind later.

options.title: Diversify before lock-in
options.label: The better answer is multiple suppliers, portable standards, and contract terms that keep one provider from becoming decisive.

options.title: Pool regionally first
options.label: Regional procurement and shared infrastructure may be slower, but they can widen bargaining room more than a fast bilateral deal.

items.title: Allied subsidy races
items.prompt: What should carry the most weight when close partners back the same strategic sectors?
items.scene: Close partners are subsidizing the same semiconductor and AI sectors, risking duplication and political backlash. Some see healthy redundancy; others see a preventable race for symbolic industrial wins.
items.whyHard: A bit of redundancy can be useful, but too much turns allied resilience into allied competition for the same bottlenecks.

contextBullets.label: Actor / stake
contextBullets.text: Governments want both strategic depth and domestic political credit, even when those goals conflict.

contextBullets.label: Uncertainty
contextBullets.text: It is unclear where resilience ends and expensive duplication begins.

options.title: Accept some duplication
options.label: Strategic industries are too important to optimize only for efficiency. Some overlap is the price of resilience.

options.title: Negotiate specialization
options.label: Partners gain more from complementary roles than from spending public money to outbid each other in the same sectors.

options.title: Keep national depth
options.label: Specialization is useful, but no government wants to discover too late that its most strategic capacity lives abroad.

options.title: Let market discipline sort
options.label: Public subsidy races can spend enormous sums on political symbolism while crowding out more adaptive private investment.

items.title: Regional public compute
items.prompt: What should carry the most weight when middle powers consider a shared compute buildout?
items.scene: Several middle powers are debating whether to pool public compute, cloud capacity, and training programs instead of each chasing a national frontier stack. Finance ministries want scale. Security officials worry pooled systems could dilute control.
items.whyHard: National buildout is politically cleaner, but separate national stacks may be too thin to matter. A regional pool can solve scale and still create new coordination risks.

contextBullets.label: Actor / stake
contextBullets.text: These states want more capacity, but none can cheaply build every frontier layer alone.

contextBullets.label: Uncertainty
contextBullets.text: It is unclear whether durable capacity comes from national depth, pooled scale, targeted public layers, or letting private actors sort it out.

options.title: Keep national depth
options.label: Shared access is useful, but strategic sectors still need national control over their most critical compute and cloud layers.

options.title: Pool scale regionally
options.label: A shared buildout is the strongest path because scale, talent, and bargaining power all improve when middle powers stop duplicating thin national efforts.

options.title: Fund the missing layers
options.label: The smarter approach is targeted public support for power, cloud access, and training rather than one grand frontier gesture.

options.title: Let the market choose
options.label: Governments should widen access and basic infrastructure, but they should not guess too confidently which compute model will age best.

items.title: Model incidents and mandatory reporting
items.prompt: What should matter most after a serious model incident?
items.scene: A frontier model contributes to a serious cyber and biosecurity incident. Governments now debate whether reporting should become mandatory, whether sensitive details should stay national, and whether liability should shift toward deployers rather than model developers alone.
items.whyHard: Disclosure can make safety governance real, but it can also expose information that governments and firms do not want to standardize publicly.

contextBullets.label: Actor / stake
contextBullets.text: The incident has made the gap between voluntary safety talk and enforceable governance impossible to ignore.

contextBullets.label: Uncertainty
contextBullets.text: Too little disclosure preserves opacity; too much may create new security problems or freeze cooperation.

options.title: Mandate shared reporting
options.label: Serious incidents should trigger common disclosure and audit baselines or governance will remain mostly rhetorical.

options.title: Keep sensitive reporting national
options.label: Governments should require reporting, but the most consequential incidents belong in controlled national channels rather than broad shared disclosure.

options.title: Shift liability to deployment
options.label: The better lever is to make downstream deployers bear more responsibility instead of assuming model developers are the only governance choke point.

options.title: Avoid overgeneralizing
options.label: A serious incident matters, but rushing to one broad reporting regime may harden rules before the causal picture is actually clear.

items.title: AI standards without broad voice
items.prompt: What is the deeper issue when a small club starts setting global AI standards?
items.scene: A club of technically capable states is close to setting AI testing and deployment standards that many others will have to live with. Supporters say only capable states can move fast enough. Critics say the process will set global defaults without broad voice.
items.whyHard: A narrow club may be easier to enforce, but that does not settle whether others will see the rules as legitimate, development-friendly, or compatible with regulatory autonomy.

contextBullets.label: Actor / stake
contextBullets.text: The standards will shape access, compliance costs, and deployment rules far beyond the states writing them.

contextBullets.label: Uncertainty
contextBullets.text: It is unclear whether the bigger risk is weak enforcement, weak legitimacy, hidden development costs, or reduced national room to govern.

options.title: Capable states must lead
options.label: The first requirement is enforceable standards, and only a narrow set of states currently has the technical and regulatory capacity to build them fast enough.

options.title: Legitimacy needs broader voice
options.label: Rules that others must live under will be weaker in the long run if the writers treat broad participation as optional.

options.title: The development costs are hidden
options.label: The sharper issue is that compliance costs and access barriers may fall hardest on states that were barely in the room when the rules were drafted.

options.title: Regulatory room still matters
options.label: A state may want common baselines and still resist standards that narrow domestic room to govern its own deployment choices.
